title: Ticket clustering found 4 issue types — route tickets by cluster ID?

scenario.role: You're the support-ops analyst at Norwell
scenario.situation: The support-ops team clustered incoming tickets on two features derived from ticket text — urgency_score and complexity_score — into 4 "issue type" clusters (k=4, chosen from an elbow plot), and wants to auto-route new tickets by cluster ID starting Monday, skipping the current keyword-based router entirely.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "We clustered tickets into 4 issue types. Let's route by cluster ID starting Monday — it's more accurate than the old keyword rules."
scenario.question: Is the 4-cluster issue-type assignment stable enough to route tickets by — the same clustering you'd get if you re-ran the job tomorrow — or would a re-run send tickets to different queues? Check reproducibility before the router switches over.

columns.name: cluster_run1
columns.description: K-means(k=4) cluster label from the first run, fit on urgency_score/complexity_score (standardized)

columns.name: cluster_run2
columns.description: K-means(k=4) cluster label from a second run — same tickets, same k, only the random initialization differs. Labels are pre-matched to run1's numbering for comparison.

guidingQuestions: What share of tickets have the same cluster_run1 and cluster_run2? (Labels are already matched, so a direct equality check is valid.)
For tickets that changed cluster between runs, where do urgency_score and complexity_score sit — near the middle of the data, or out at the extremes?
Plot (or describe) urgency_score vs. complexity_score. Do 4 visually distinct groups actually appear, or a continuous, overlapping cloud?
If routing switches to cluster_run1 tomorrow and someone re-runs the exact same clustering job next week, how many tickets would land in a different queue than they did today?
What would a support-ops team need to see before trusting cluster ID as a routing key instead of the current keyword rules?
suggestedApproach: Compute the share of tickets where cluster_run1 == cluster_run2 — the reproducibility rate.
Isolate tickets that switched clusters and check whether they sit near cluster boundaries rather than scattered randomly.
Visualize (or bucket) urgency_score against complexity_score and look for 4 genuinely separated groups versus one overlapping cloud.
Consider whether the data actually supports 4 groups, or a smaller number.
Frame the operational risk: a ticket router that sends roughly 1 in 4 tickets to a different queue than it would have a week earlier, with nothing in the ticket having changed.

teachingNote.naiveRead: K-means found 4 clean issue-type clusters, and they look ready to route on — swap the keyword rules for cluster ID and let the model decide the queue.
teachingNote.theTrap: K-means converges to whichever partition is nearest its random starting point, not necessarily one true global answer — and when the underlying data doesn't actually contain 4 cleanly separated groups (this ticket population is really closer to 2 broad, overlapping flavors, with k=4 picked from an elbow-plot ritual rather than real structure), the extra clusters get carved out of the overlapping middle wherever the random initialization happens to land. Re-run the identical clustering on the identical tickets, changing only the random seed, and 28% of tickets land in a different cluster than before. Cluster ID here isn't measuring a stable property of the ticket — a large share of it is just which random start the algorithm happened to get that day.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Before routing on cluster ID, check reproducibility: re-run the clustering (different seed, same tickets) and measure agreement. Here only about 72% of tickets keep the same cluster (adjusted Rand index ≈ 0.49 between runs) — real instability, not rounding noise, and far too shaky to hand routing decisions to. The honest move is either to stabilize the method (many more random restarts with a consensus/majority-vote label, or a routing model trained with labeled ground truth instead of unsupervised clusters) or to check whether the ticket population actually supports 4 issue types — here it looks closer to 2. Tell the team: don't cut over the router to cluster_run1 as-is. A router that reshuffles a quarter of its own decisions on a re-run, with nothing about the tickets having changed, will misroute constantly and be nearly impossible to debug.
howToGetThere: Re-run k-means(k=4) on the identical ticket data with only the random seed changed; match cluster labels between runs by maximum overlap (Hungarian algorithm).
Compute the share of tickets with the same matched cluster in both runs: ≈ 72% — meaning 28% reshuffle.
Compute the adjusted Rand index between the two runs: ≈ 0.49 — well below 1.0, confirming real instability.
Visualize urgency_score vs. complexity_score: the population forms one broad, overlapping cloud rather than 4 visually separated groups.
Conclude: k=4 doesn't reflect genuine structure here; cluster ID is not a stable enough signal to route production tickets on as-is.

numbers.label: Tickets with the same cluster across two re-runs
Tickets reassigned to a different cluster
Adjusted Rand index between the two runs
Genuinely separated groups visible in the data

teachingNote.lesson: K-means always returns exactly k clusters, whether or not the data actually contains k separated groups — and when it doesn't, the extra boundaries are drawn wherever the random initialization lands, not by any real structure. Before making an operational decision (routing, budget, targeting) depend on a clustering result, re-run it with a different seed and measure agreement. Low reproducibility isn't a bug to shrug off — it's the clustering telling you the number of groups you asked for isn't the number of groups that's actually there.
